questions.stem: Examine these statements: Which two are true?

codeBlocks.title: PL/SQL and SQL statements

options.text: The bank_activity_proc will not compile because of the commit.
options.explanation: An autonomous procedure may issue COMMIT for its own independent transaction. The COMMIT shown is not, by itself, a compilation error.

options.text: Both tables will have a row inserted and committed.
options.explanation: The outer bank_transaction insert is not committed in the shown flow. The final ROLLBACK reverses that insert, while the autonomous bank_activity insert was committed independently.

options.text: The transaction for the bank_activity_proc is independent of the bank_transaction_proc.
options.explanation: PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION gives bank_activity_proc its own transaction. Its COMMIT applies to that transaction without committing the caller’s bank_transaction insert.

options.text: Only one table will have a row inserted and committed.
options.explanation: bank_activity_proc commits its insert into BANK_ACTIVITY. The final ROLLBACK undoes the uncommitted BANK_TRANSACTION insert, leaving only the BANK_ACTIVITY row committed.

options.text: Neither table will have a row inserted and committed.
options.explanation: The final ROLLBACK cannot undo the autonomous transaction already committed by bank_activity_proc, so BANK_ACTIVITY retains its row.

questions.answerExplanation: PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION gives bank_activity_proc its own transaction. Its COMMIT applies to that transaction without committing the caller’s bank_transaction insert. bank_activity_proc commits its insert into BANK_ACTIVITY. The final ROLLBACK undoes the uncommitted BANK_TRANSACTION insert, leaving only the BANK_ACTIVITY row committed.
questions.feedback: The caller inserts into BANK_TRANSACTION but does not commit. It calls bank_activity_proc, whose AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION pragma starts an independent transaction; that procedure inserts into BANK_ACTIVITY and commits. After control returns, the final ROLLBACK undoes the caller’s pending insert only.

questions.stem: Which two are true about the PLSQL_CODE_TYPE parameter?

options.text: If set to NATIVE programs are stored in a PL/SQL bytecode format.
options.explanation: NATIVE compiles eligible stored PL/SQL units to native machine code. INTERPRETED is the setting associated with PL/SQL bytecode.

options.text: Changing the parameter setting automatically changes the setting for existing _____ units.
options.explanation: Changing PLSQL_CODE_TYPE does not retroactively change already compiled units. The missing word in the image does not change that rule.

options.text: If set to NATIVE, programs are stored in platform dependent machine code.
options.explanation: NATIVE compiles eligible PL/SQL library units to native machine code, which runs without the interpreter. This contrasts with INTERPRETED bytecode.

options.text: It can use the reuse settings clause to recompile a program unit without changing the current session settings.
options.explanation: ALTER ... COMPILE REUSE SETTINGS recompiles using settings already stored with the program unit rather than replacing them with the current session compilation settings.

options.text: The default value is NATIVE.
options.explanation: Oracle documents INTERPRETED as the default value for PLSQL_CODE_TYPE, not NATIVE.

questions.answerExplanation: NATIVE compiles eligible PL/SQL library units to native machine code, which runs without the interpreter. This contrasts with INTERPRETED bytecode. ALTER ... COMPILE REUSE SETTINGS recompiles using settings already stored with the program unit rather than replacing them with the current session compilation settings.
questions.feedback: PLSQL_CODE_TYPE is a compilation setting, not a switch that changes already compiled code. INTERPRETED means bytecode executed by the PL/SQL interpreter; NATIVE means eligible library units compile to native machine code. REUSE SETTINGS concerns which saved compiler settings a recompile uses.

questions.stem: Which two are true about named notations in a PL/SQL subprogram?

options.text: The actual parameter must be specified in the same order as the formal parameter declared.
options.explanation: Named notation associates an argument with a formal parameter by name (formal_name => value). The caller can therefore supply named arguments in a different order.

options.text: Only trailing optional parameters can be omitted in the invocation call.
options.explanation: With named notation, any parameter that has a default can be omitted, even if it appears between required parameters; the default supplies its value.

options.text: Specifying actual parameters in the wrong order results in the subprogram terminating without exception.
options.explanation: Named notation does not rely on positional order, so a different order is not itself an error. Missing required arguments or wrong names/types can instead prevent a valid call.

options.text: The subprogram invocations must be changed when the formal parameter list acquires new required parameters.
options.explanation: A new required parameter has no default, so an existing invocation that omits it no longer supplies every required argument. Update the call to pass the new named parameter.

options.text: Any optional parameters can be omitted in the invocation call.
options.explanation: An optional formal parameter has a default value. Named notation lets the caller omit that parameter wherever it appears in the declaration, allowing the default to apply.

questions.answerExplanation: A new required parameter has no default, so an existing invocation that omits it no longer supplies every required argument. Update the call to pass the new named parameter. An optional formal parameter has a default value. Named notation lets the caller omit that parameter wherever it appears in the declaration, allowing the default to apply.
questions.feedback: Formal parameters are declared by the subprogram; actual arguments are supplied at a call. Named notation uses formal_name => value, so argument order is flexible. A parameter with a default is optional, but one without a default must still be supplied.

questions.stem: Which is true about counter variables in a FOR loop?

options.text: It cannot be NULL.
options.explanation: The numeric FOR-loop index is generated from the numeric range and receives an integer value on each iteration; it is not a user-declared nullable variable. If the loop executes no iterations, no loop-index value is available outside it.

options.text: It can be modified in the body of the loop.
options.explanation: The loop controls its own index. Code inside the loop can read it but cannot assign a new value to it.

options.text: It must explicitly be declared.
options.explanation: PL/SQL implicitly declares the numeric FOR-loop index in the loop header. You do not declare it separately.

options.text: It is accessible outside the body of the loop.
options.explanation: The implicitly declared loop index is local to the FOR loop. Statements after END LOOP cannot refer to that loop index.

questions.answerExplanation: The numeric FOR-loop index is generated from the numeric range and receives an integer value on each iteration; it is not a user-declared nullable variable. If the loop executes no iterations, no loop-index value is available outside it.
questions.feedback: In FOR i IN 1..5 LOOP, PL/SQL creates i automatically and gives it the successive integer values 1 through 5. The body may read i, but it cannot assign to i; after the loop, that loop-local i is out of scope.

items.sql: GRANT EXECUTE ON proc1 TO ora2;

sections.title: Additional context
sections.content: User ora2 has password ora2 in pdb1.

options.explanation: The script connects as ora2 and calls the procedure owned by ora1 using `ora1.proc1(x)`. This matches the procedure's owner in the setup and passes writable variable x for its OUT NUMBER parameter. An OUT parameter does not receive x's initial value of 5, so the procedure's `v1 * 10` expression does not print 50; this does not make the procedure call invalid.
A procedure does not return a value to assign to x, and this call does not supply the required OUT argument. A valid call would pass a writable variable to the procedure as an argument.

The shown procedure requires an OUT argument, but none is supplied. Also, EXEC is a client command, not a PL/SQL statement to place inside BEGIN ... END; call proc1(x) with a declared variable instead.
Qualifying the owner does not remove the required OUT parameter. EXEC is a client command rather than a PL/SQL statement inside a block, so the shown block does not make a valid procedure call.

questions.answerExplanation: Choice A is the reviewer-highlighted script. It connects as ora2, uses the granted EXECUTE privilege to call `ora1.proc1(x)`, and supplies a writable variable for the OUT parameter. The procedure does not assign v1 before reading it, so its multiplication uses NULL; the question asks which script executes successfully, not which prints 50.
questions.technicalNote: Choice A's `ora1.proc1(x)` is schema-qualified, matching the procedure created by ora1 and the EXECUTE grant to ora2. The OUT parameter does not receive x's initial value of 5, and the procedure does not assign v1 before evaluating `v1 * 10`; this affects output, not the source-highlighted choice's validity as a procedure call.
questions.feedback: First, ora1 creates `proc1(v1 OUT NUMBER)` and grants ora2 permission to execute it. Choice A connects as ora2, declares x, and calls `ora1.proc1(x)`. The `ora1.` prefix identifies the procedure's owner; `x` is a writable actual argument for OUT. The OUT parameter is not initialized from x's value of 5, so `v1 * 10` uses NULL. The highlighted choice does not contain a later `DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(x)` call.

questions.stem: Which three are true about anonymous blocks and subprograms?

options.text: Named subprograms are stored in the database server.
options.explanation: Stored standalone or packaged subprograms are compiled database objects. This contrasts with an anonymous block, which is not saved as a named program unit.

options.text: A FUNCTION subprogram must return one or more values.
options.explanation: A function has a RETURN type and must return a value along a successful execution path. The image says one or more values; technically, one RETURN value may itself be a composite value such as a record.

options.text: Named subprograms cannot be called from other packages.
options.explanation: Public subprograms in a package specification can be called from other packages when accessible and appropriately privileged.

options.text: FUNCTION subprograms must be called and pass through one or more parameters.
options.explanation: A function can be declared with no parameters and invoked without supplying arguments. Parameters are optional.

options.text: PROCEDURE subprograms can accept parameters.
options.explanation: A procedure can declare IN, OUT, or IN OUT parameters so callers can pass values in or receive values out; parameters are optional, not mandatory.

options.text: Anonymous blocks must always start with the Declare keyword.
options.explanation: DECLARE is optional when there are no declarations; an anonymous PL/SQL block may begin directly with BEGIN.

options.text: Anonymous blocks cannot use packaged variables.
options.explanation: A package specification can expose public variables, which an anonymous block can reference with the package name when accessible.

questions.answerExplanation: Stored standalone or packaged subprograms are compiled database objects. This contrasts with an anonymous block, which is not saved as a named program unit. A function has a RETURN type and must return a value along a successful execution path. The image says one or more values; technically, one RETURN value may itself be a composite value such as a record. A procedure can declare IN, OUT, or IN OUT parameters so callers can pass values in or receive values out; parameters are optional, not mandatory.
questions.technicalNote: Choice B says a function returns "one or more values." A PL/SQL function returns one value through RETURN; that single value can be composite, such as a record containing multiple fields. The highlighted choice is true only if "one or more" includes the one-value case; it does not mean a function can return multiple separate RETURN values.
questions.feedback: A named stored subprogram is a reusable function or procedure kept in the database; an anonymous block has no stored name. A function returns one value (which may contain several fields), while a procedure performs an action and may use parameters. Both can be invoked from other PL/SQL code when accessible.

questions.stem: Which statement is true about user-defined records?

options.text: They can be returned from a function.
options.explanation: A function can return a value of a PL/SQL record type when the type is declared in a scope accessible to the function and caller. The returned record can contain multiple fields.

options.text: The number of fields must match the number of columns in a table.
options.explanation: A user-defined RECORD can have any fields the programmer declares. It need not represent a full table row; matching a table row is associated with %ROWTYPE or a particular assignment.

options.text: Field names must match selected column names.
options.explanation: A user-defined record’s field names are chosen in its type declaration. A SELECT INTO can populate it when the selected values match the record fields by position and compatible type; names need not match.

options.text: Field types must match column types.
options.explanation: A record can contain fields not tied to any table. When fetching selected values into it, corresponding data types must be compatible, not necessarily identically declared column types.

questions.answerExplanation: A function can return a value of a PL/SQL record type when the type is declared in a scope accessible to the function and caller. The returned record can contain multiple fields.
questions.feedback: A RECORD groups named fields that can have different data types. A user-defined record is designed in PL/SQL, not automatically constrained to a table’s column count, names, or exact declared types. A function can return a record as one composite result.

questions.stem: Which three are true regarding code based access control (CBAC)?

options.text: You can CBAC to attach database roles to a PL/SQL function, procedure, or package.
options.explanation: CBAC grants a database role to a stored PL/SQL program unit, enabling that role while the unit executes. The source wording “You can CBAC” is retained as shown.

options.text: You can CBAC to attach database roles to a PL/SQL function or procedure only.
options.explanation: CBAC also supports PL/SQL packages, so “only” makes this statement too narrow.

options.text: CBAC roles can be granted to a unit program only if they are the predefined roles automatically defined by the standard scripts as part of database creation.
options.explanation: The screenshot highlights this statement, but Oracle says eligible roles are standard database roles directly granted to the owner; they are not limited to roles predefined by database-creation scripts. This is a source-answer conflict, not a rule to memorize.

options.text: CBAC cannot be used secure definer's rights.
options.explanation: Oracle explicitly documents CBAC for both definer’s-rights and invoker’s-rights program units, so “cannot” is false.

options.text: In a multitenant environment, the DELEGATE option of CBAC cannot be used.
options.explanation: Oracle describes DELEGATE as an option relevant to CBAC grants. The screenshot gives no basis for an absolute multitenant prohibition; treat the blanket “cannot” claim as unsupported.

options.text: In CBAC, the ADMIN and DELEGATE options cannot both be granted to the same user.
options.explanation: The source does not highlight this statement. The ADMIN and DELEGATE options describe grant authority; Oracle’s CBAC guidance does not establish the asserted blanket prohibition.

options.text: CBAC roles can be granted to a program unit only if they are directly granted to its owner.
options.explanation: Oracle lists direct grant of the role to the program-unit owner as a condition for CBAC role grants. The grantor also needs the relevant authority; a direct owner grant alone is not the whole checklist.

questions.answerExplanation: CBAC grants a database role to a stored PL/SQL program unit, enabling that role while the unit executes. The source wording “You can CBAC” is retained as shown. The screenshot highlights this statement, but Oracle says eligible roles are standard database roles directly granted to the owner; they are not limited to roles predefined by database-creation scripts. This is a source-answer conflict, not a rule to memorize. Oracle lists direct grant of the role to the program-unit owner as a condition for CBAC role grants. The grantor also needs the relevant authority; a direct owner grant alone is not the whole checklist.
questions.technicalNote: Choice C is highlighted, but its "only predefined roles" restriction is not a CBAC requirement. Oracle permits standard database roles directly granted to the program-unit owner, subject to grantor authority; such roles are not limited to roles predefined by database-creation scripts. Therefore choice C conflicts with the documented rule, while choice G states the direct-grant requirement.
questions.feedback: CBAC means Code Based Access Control: attach a database role to a PL/SQL function, procedure, or package so its privileges are enabled when that unit runs. To grant such a role, Oracle specifies grantor/owner authority and direct grants of eligible standard database roles to the program-unit owner.

options.text: Only the PRICE column can be updated in the products table.
options.explanation: FOR UPDATE OF price does not prohibit updating other columns. The shown UPDATE changes PRICE because its SET clause names price, not because the cursor limits all possible updates to that column.

options.text: The FOR UPDATE OF clause can be used only if the WHERE CURRENT clause is --- executable part of the block.
options.explanation: FOR UPDATE OF can be used without a WHERE CURRENT OF update. The dependency goes the other way: a positioned WHERE CURRENT OF update needs a FOR UPDATE cursor. The garbled words are retained from the screenshot.

options.text: The WHERE CURRENT OF clause can be used only if the FOR UPDATE clause is used in the cursor definition.
options.explanation: WHERE CURRENT OF c1 targets the cursor’s current row for an UPDATE or DELETE. c1 must be a FOR UPDATE cursor, as it is in the shown declaration.

options.text: The lock acquired when executing the OPEN c1 command will be released only a COMMIT or ROLLBACK statement is issued.
options.explanation: Opening a FOR UPDATE cursor locks the selected rows. In this transaction, those locks are released when COMMIT or ROLLBACK ends the transaction; closing the cursor alone does not commit or roll back.

options.text: An OPEN c1 command will acquire a lock only on the PRICE column in the PRODUCT ---.
options.explanation: Oracle locks rows selected by the FOR UPDATE cursor, not just a column. OF price identifies a column of the table whose rows are locked; it does not create a PRICE-only column lock.

questions.answerExplanation: WHERE CURRENT OF c1 targets the cursor’s current row for an UPDATE or DELETE. c1 must be a FOR UPDATE cursor, as it is in the shown declaration. Opening a FOR UPDATE cursor locks the selected rows. In this transaction, those locks are released when COMMIT or ROLLBACK ends the transaction; closing the cursor alone does not commit or roll back.
questions.feedback: c1 selects rows from PRODUCTS for a positioned update. FOR UPDATE OF price locks selected rows when the cursor is opened; it does not lock only PRICE or restrict the columns that can be updated. WHERE CURRENT OF c1 identifies the current row after it has been fetched. The image shows fragments, not the OPEN/FETCH steps of a complete executable block.

questions.stem: Which three are true about the procedure overloading features?

options.text: Each procedure's formal parameters can differ in data type or name.
options.explanation: Overloads share a procedure name but may have formal parameters that differ in type family or name (as well as number or order). When they differ only in name, named notation can distinguish them.

options.text: Each procedure must use positional notation to specify the corresponding actual parameters.
options.explanation: This is highlighted in the source, but positional notation is not required. When overloads differ only by formal-parameter names, positional notation cannot disambiguate them; named notation is required for that call.

options.text: Each procedure must use named notation to specify the corresponding actual parameters.
options.explanation: Named notation is needed for overloads that differ only in formal-parameter names, but it is not required for every overloaded call. Overloads distinguishable by data type or number may be called positionally.

options.text: Each procedure can be a packaged subprogram.
options.explanation: A package can contain multiple procedures with the same name and distinguishable formal parameters. The package specification declares the overloads and the body defines them.

options.text: Each procedure can be a standalone subprogram.
options.explanation: Standalone procedures with the same schema-level name do not coexist as separate overloads; creating one with CREATE OR REPLACE replaces the earlier standalone object.

options.text: Each procedure's formal parameters must differ in name.
options.explanation: Parameter names do not always have to differ: differences in parameter number, order, or data type family can distinguish overloads.

options.text: Each procedure can be a nested subprogram.
options.explanation: PL/SQL supports overloading nested subprograms declared within the same enclosing scope. This statement is technically true even though it is not highlighted.

questions.answerExplanation: Overloads share a procedure name but may have formal parameters that differ in type family or name (as well as number or order). When they differ only in name, named notation can distinguish them. This is highlighted in the source, but positional notation is not required. When overloads differ only by formal-parameter names, positional notation cannot disambiguate them; named notation is required for that call. A package can contain multiple procedures with the same name and distinguishable formal parameters. The package specification declares the overloads and the body defines them.
questions.technicalNote: Choice B is highlighted but contradicts Oracle’s rule: named notation, not positional notation, is required when overloaded formal parameters differ only by name. Choice G is not highlighted although Oracle explicitly permits overloaded nested subprograms. The source asks for three, but the highlighted set is not technically consistent.
questions.feedback: Overloading gives multiple procedures the same name in a package or nested scope, with distinguishable parameter lists. The call can use positional or named notation when unambiguous; if the only difference is parameter names, named notation selects the intended overload.
